y ~ finite_mixture(lambda,

increment_log_prob(finite_mixture(lambda,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: [stan] add syntax for mixtures of distributions (#583)
parts:
I think that's a challenge to explain increment_log_prob()
and the way Stan works more clearly.

There are three confusing aspects:

1. The sampling notation ~ doesn't literally sample the left
side from the distribution on the right --- it just increments
the log probability.

2. Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.

3. The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
notation version does.

All three points have led to a great deal of confusion.

One thing I'd like to do is have a version of the "_log"-suffixed
functions that does drop constant terms, so I can say something like:

y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

is equivalent to:

increment_log_prob(normal_log_propto(y,mu,sigma));

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: [stan] add syntax for mixtures of distributions (#583)
parts:
On Saturday, March 1, 2014 3:13:38 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I think that's a challenge to explain increment_log_prob()
and the way Stan works more clearly.

There are three confusing aspects:

1.  The sampling notation ~ doesn't literally sample the left
side from the distribution on the right --- it just increments
the log probability.

I think, in retrospect, it may have been a mistake to make the syntax the same as BUGS when what it means is very different from what BUGS means. In my class, we are learning Stan before BUGS, so we'll see if the students get confused the other way..
2.  Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.

This is pretty straightforward I think if you understand point 1, which is to say that you understand that Stan is not a Gibbs sampler and need to work with PDFs of distributions rather than merely PRNGs for distributions.

3.  The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
notation version does.

This is big-time confusing, particularly because people need the constants sometimes. I still think it would be relatively easy to have Stan calculate the log posterior once with constants included, once with constants excluded, cache the difference, and then initialize the quantity formerly known as lp__ to that in subsequent iterations. That way, we don't waste (much) time calculating constants but we remove the inconsistency in the output. Then we just have to remind people of the hidden Jacobian terms.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
[changed subject]

"Leaky" sounds like a bad thing! I see the term derives
from Joel Spolsky, who has a knack for catchy naming:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaky_abstraction

I like to think of the abstraction here as being that
the model defines a log probability function over
parameters up to a constant. As such, I view the
sampling statements not so much as an abstraction as
syntactic sugar for the direct increment.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntactic_sugar

Stan's given users the ability to manipulate lp__ from the
beginning. That's been deprecated and hidden behind
increment_log_prob() and sampling statement syntax, both
of which do provide a layer of abstraction over manipulating
the log probability accumulator lp__ directly.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: [stan] add syntax for mixtures of distributions (#583)
parts:
On Mar 1, 2014, at 9:20 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Saturday, March 1, 2014 3:13:38 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I think that's a challenge to explain increment_log_prob()
> and the way Stan works more clearly.
>
> There are three confusing aspects:
>
> 1. The sampling notation ~ doesn't literally sample the left
> side from the distribution on the right --- it just increments
> the log probability.
>
> I think, in retrospect, it may have been a mistake to make the syntax the same as BUGS when what it means is very different from what BUGS means. In my class, we are learning Stan before BUGS, so we'll see if the students get confused the other way..

But BUGS doesn't mean direct sampling either!

In BUGS/JAGS, the sampling statements and assignments define
(roughly) a directed acyclic graph. And then the Markov blanket
of a node lets you define conditional distribution for it with which
you can do Gibbs sampling (or an approximation thereof, like slice
sampling):

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_blanket

> 2. Suffixing "_log" to a distribution name gives you a function.
>
> This is pretty straightforward I think if you understand point 1, which is to say that you understand that Stan is not a Gibbs sampler and need to work with PDFs of distributions rather than merely PRNGs for distributions.

I don't think anyone can get by with PRNGs only, unless they
want to build a big and inefficient rejection sampler!

Languages like Church have an interesting take on this where
the equivalent of the sampling statements in BUGS or Stan
are kind of like direct statements, but also kind of not like
them because they do something like Metropolis over execution
paths (in a way I still don't fully comprehend --- if someone has
a pointer to an explanation of how sampling actually works in Church,
please post it).

> 3. The function doesn't drop constant terms and the sampling
> notation version does.
>
> This is big-time confusing, particularly because people need the constants sometimes. I still think it would be relatively easy to have Stan calculate the log posterior once with constants included, once with constants excluded, cache the difference, and then initialize the quantity formerly known as lp__ to that in subsequent iterations. That way, we don't waste (much) time calculating constants but we remove the inconsistency in the output. Then we just have to remind people of the hidden Jacobian terms.

That's a great idea and there's no way to do it efficiently
direclty within Stan as it is. Had we been more concerned with model comparison
at the get go, we probably would've built that in.

No reason we can't do that now, so I created an issue for it:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/584

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: [stan] add syntax for mixtures of distributions (#583)
parts:
The way it was explained to me was that you translate
the posterior evaluation into an expression graph where
each evaluation is a random function.  So instead of
assigning a node to, say, f(x), it gets the random value
f ~ pi(x).  Then you can resample by selecting a node,
resampling a value, and propagating that down the graph
resampling until you hit the end of the graph.

The values at the end are then used as a Metropolis proposal
to compensate for any approximate sampling used instead
of exact sampling.

On Mar 1, 2014, at 10:42 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Languages like Church have an interesting take on this where
the equivalent of the sampling statements in BUGS or Stan 
are kind of like direct statements, but also kind of not like
them because they do something like Metropolis over execution
paths (in a way I still don't fully comprehend --- if someone has
a pointer to an explanation of how sampling actually works in Church,
please post it).

See the discussion at
http://blog.codinghorror.com/all-abstractions-are-failed-abstractions/
especially this bit:

Instead, let's ask ourselves a more pragmatic question: Does this
abstraction make our code at least a little easier to write? To
understand? To troubleshoot? Are we better off with this abstraction
than we were without it?

Stan is a DSL (domain-specific language), and a particularly good
one. The ~ abstraction is very useful in this problem domain
(statistics), because it allows us to say what we mean. I see no major
problem with it being a bit "leaky".

That said, I think that the biggest leak is when one needs to manually
correct for Jacobians. But it is reasonable to assume that users of Stan
have some training in basic probability (no need to be a statistician,
just having taken an more or less advanced undergrad course is enough
IMO) so as long as we can't come up with a more abstract solution for
this it is fine.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
On Mar 2, 2014, at 12:01 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> ...

> That said, I think that the biggest leak is when one needs to manually
> correct for Jacobians. But it is reasonable to assume that users of Stan
> have some training in basic probability (no need to be a statistician,
> just having taken an more or less advanced undergrad course is enough
> IMO) so as long as we can't come up with a more abstract solution for
> this it is fine.

Setting aside the semantics of what the "abstraction" is and whether
it is "leaky" or not, we could mitigate the problem of having to specify
Jacobians by exposing a class of transform functions that automatically
compute and apply the Jacobian. That's what our constrained variables
already do. In order to make it clean, we'd have to allow it to be used
in transformed data and generated quantities blocks that do not require
Jacobians by just skipping that part of the transform.

The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
of the language. I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:

y <- log(x)
y ~ normal(mu,sigma)

because you wind up having two parents for the node y.

I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
in generated quantities. These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
expressions context-dependent in their use.

The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
out the Markov blanket of a parameter.

- Bob

> compute and apply the Jacobian. That's what our constrained variables
> already do. In order to make it clean, we'd have to allow it to be used
> in transformed data and generated quantities blocks that do not require
> Jacobians by just skipping that part of the transform.

Why should this functionality be restricted to a class of transform
functions? I guess all bijections could be supported.

> The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
> statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
> do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
> of the language. I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:
>
> y <- log(x)
> y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
>
> because you wind up having two parents for the node y.

I could imagine a different syntax for a transformation, eg some
character that is not used for anything else but is different from <-
and ~. Let's imagine for a moment that it's, say, \, then

y \ log(x)

would mean "adjust the posterior according to the Jacobian correction."

> I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
> used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
> we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
> The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
> in generated quantities. These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
> expressions context-dependent in their use.

I imagine that in the long run Stan could be organized into layers: the
bottom layer would simply be an engine for specifying a function (the
posterior), with some bare syntax (eg an enumeration of terms that need
to be added to it, no ~, no Jacobians, etc), then layers on top of that
could implement convenience forms (eg ~, Jacobians) that transform into
bottom layer code. Users would rarely ever need to see the bottom layer
for simple code (much like manipulations of lp__ are rarely needed in
simple cases).

I expect that this approach would benefit a lot from Stan being a
declarative/functional language, instead of the current
declarative/imperative mix. I am not familiar with the details of the
implementation, but I am wondering if re-assigning variables really buys
anything in terms of speed or ease of implementation.

> The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
> Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
> out the Markov blanket of a parameter.

I think that this is something orthogonal to the issue we discussed in
this thread, but maybe I misunderstand.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions.

I agree that it'd make sense to call out the Jacobian adjustment
if it happens. It's definitely in the "advanced" category --- I
was using BUGS happily before I even understood what a Jacobian was.

To clarify, Stan is 100% imperative. The sampling statements may
appear to be declarative, but they're purely imperative --- they just
increment the log probabilty function and are executed imperatively in
the order they are found.

There's are presently no functional components to Stan --- nothing
where you can pass a function to another function or in any way treat
functions as first-class objects.

You're right --- not being able to sample integers is orthogonal
to sampling statements vs. increment_log_prob statements.

- Bob

> functions? I guess all bijections could be supported.
>
>> The syntax of allowing expressions on the left-hand side of sampling
>> statements could be restricted to just variables or constants, as BUGS/JAGS
>> do, and that would in some sense "plug the leak" by reducing the expressiveness
>> of the language. I don't think BUGS or JAGS let you do this if x is a parameter:
>>
>> y <- log(x)
>> y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
>>
>> because you wind up having two parents for the node y.
>
> I could imagine a different syntax for a transformation, eg some
> character that is not used for anything else but is different from <-
> and ~. Let's imagine for a moment that it's, say, \, then
>
> y \ log(x)
>
> would mean "adjust the posterior according to the Jacobian correction."
>
>> I think the "leakiest" part of Stan's sampling abstraction is that "~" can only be
>> used in the model (it could potentially be used in transformed parameters, but
>> we decided to disallow it thinking it would be clearer restricted to the model).
>> The "leaky" part of the function abstraction is that (P)RNG functions can only be used
>> in generated quantities. These restrictions respectively makes the statements and
>> expressions context-dependent in their use.
>
> I imagine that in the long run Stan could be organized into layers: the
> bottom layer would simply be an engine for specifying a function (the
> posterior), with some bare syntax (eg an enumeration of terms that need
> to be added to it, no ~, no Jacobians, etc), then layers on top of that
> could implement convenience forms (eg ~, Jacobians) that transform into
> bottom layer code. Users would rarely ever need to see the bottom layer
> for simple code (much like manipulations of lp__ are rarely needed in
> simple cases).
>
> I expect that this approach would benefit a lot from Stan being a
> declarative/functional language, instead of the current
> declarative/imperative mix. I am not familiar with the details of the
> implementation, but I am wondering if re-assigning variables really buys
> anything in terms of speed or ease of implementation.
>
>> The really really big "leak" is that we can't use integers as parameters.
>> Because we allow general log probability computations, it's impossible to pull
>> out the Markov blanket of a parameter.
>
> I think that this is something orthogonal to the issue we discussed in
> this thread, but maybe I misunderstand.
>
> Best,
>
> Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
On Mar 2, 2014, at 9:11 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I think that there is an important distinction here:
> STAN-the-implementation is clearly imperative, but STAN-the-language
> contains elements (the ~ statements) that could be understood as
> declarative (even if their implementation is imperative). Currently
> there is a single implementation (which of course makes sense), so the
> two are easily confounded.

I hadn't even thought of different implementations. If
you removed the assignment statements and increment_log_prob, you
could be left with something that's roughly declarative in the
same sense as BUGS/JAGS. In fact, that's where I started the design.
There are a lot of advantages in terms of static program analysis
(as in ML, to add another functional language to the mix).

I think a good comparison is Prolog, which masquerades as
declarative, but is in fact imperative due to the depth-first
execution order. The order of those clauses really matters,
and that's not even considering cut (! operation, not to be confused
with cut in BUGS).

> I meant another aspect of functional languages: immutable values (think
> Haskell, not CL).

Took me a while to figure out "CL" meant "Common Lisp".

The parameters and data are immutable, whereas transformed data,
transformed parameters, generated quantities, loop indices,
and local variables are all mutable (not sure having loop indices
be mutable in their bodies is really useful, though).

Maybe with inline declarations and compound declaration-definition
statements we could make everything but local variables immutable.

I'm a huge fan of immutables in coding, by the way --- I argued
at length for them in Java and have been pretty insistent that
our C++ uses immutable classes wherever possible rather than
construct-empty then apply setters. I like to be able to validate
that objects are well formed on construction and then make sure
they stay that way.

- Bob

P.S. "Stan" isn't an acronym --- no need to capitalize. I think
our all-caps logo is confusing it's not-an-acronym status, as
is Andrew's jumping in with ridiculous "bacronyms".

syntactic sugar.

having with the more complex models may be stemming from thinking of

messages.author: 5e88780fdec070b5
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
I was suggesting that at some point on the future people might build
abstraction layers on top of Stan. I believe the BayesHive folks have
already done this with BayesSig. I was referring to the addition of
functions in this proposal
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Function-Syntax-and-Semantics-Design

When I say a proper language, I mean conceptually thinking of the code
in a Stan model block as a deterministic program which produces one
sample. This extends to how I could imagine Stan semantically working
as other features from deterministic programming languages were
introduced. Now I admit that is a very narrow definition of a proper
language and I don't mean to endorse it for Stan. It's just that
mental model breaks when you encounter lp__

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
When I say a proper language, I mean conceptually thinking of the code
in a Stan model block as a deterministic program which produces one
sample.

This is a bit oxymoronic, no?  If we wanted to generate a sample (transition, whatever
you want to call it) then the code would have to be stochastic.

In any case, the model block really just defines a probability density, with
the distinction from a many-to-one function f : R^{n} -> R coming from the
need for Jacobians.  This is how it works right now and how I believe it
should continue to work in the future — I’m not convinced of the utility
of trying to abstract this away to anything else.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling syntax vs. increment_log_prob
parts:
Thanks for the clarification. I see what you mean now.

One reason I think of Stan as more of a language for defining
a log probability function is that we also use it for optimization
and are working on marginal maximal likelihood, EP and VB inference
(all of which are deterministic modulo initialization).

We're also working toward more finely articulating the log probability
function itself, such as splitting out the likelihood from the prior,
so that we can define WAIC (a nicer alternative to DIC) and splitting
up the data into batches so that we can use stochastic and parallel
inferences of various sorts.

- Bob
